text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. To begin evaluating your right ring finger, can you tell me exactly when the swelling and pain started and if there was any specific injury or trauma that preceded it?

text: 22-year-old male. The patient reports that the pain and swelling in his right ring finger began 2 days ago while playing football. He recalls his finger got caught in the jersey of another player, who then pulled away forcefully.

speaker: Doctor
text: That mechanism of injury—getting the finger caught in a jersey and pulled—is classic for a ligament sprain, often called a "jersey finger" or lateral collateral ligament injury. Can you tell me if the finger feels unstable or if it deviates to one side when you try to move it?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Progressive swelling and pain in the right ring finger. I also have Inability to flex the right ring finger at the distal interphalangeal joint when making a fist, Pain at the distal interphalangeal joint, Extended right ring finger in resting position.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for those details. To clarify the specific deficit, is it that you cannot actively bend the tip of your finger when trying to make a fist, but you can still bend it passively if I move it for you?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: X-ray of the Right Hand: No bone fractures or dislocations visible. Soft tissue swelling noted around the distal interphalangeal joint of the right ring finger.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The X-ray rules out a fracture, which is good. Since you cannot actively flex the tip of your finger but it rests extended, this strongly suggests an avulsion of the flexor tendon. Can you confirm if you feel a distinct gap or defect at the very tip of your finger on the palmar side?

speaker: Doctor
text:
The normal ultrasound is unexpected for a complete tendon rupture, but the clinical presentation of inability to actively flex the DIP joint after hyperextension trauma is classic for a Flexor Digitorum Profundus avulsion. I need to rule out a bony avulsion fragment that might have been missed or is too small for standard X-ray resolution, or confirm the tendon retraction.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Flexor Digitorum Profundus Avulsion (Jersey Finger)
